current_example.title: Example: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Column

q-36221.name: Question 1
q-36221.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & -4 & 1 \\ 0 & -5 & -5 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{32}+(-5)\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+2}|\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-5)\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -4 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 6 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

q-77481.name: Question 2
q-77481.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+3\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =3\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ -2 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

q-77483.name: Question 3
q-77483.worked_solution:
The $1$rst row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+3\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 2\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

q-69950.name: Question 4
q-69950.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 5 & -1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+2\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -3 \\ 5 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

q-130016.name: Question 5
q-130016.worked_solution:
The $1$st row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -3 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 2 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| & =5\cdot {C}_{11}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13}+0\cdot {C}_{14} \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{1+1}|\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 \\ -6 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|+2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 5 \\ 7 & 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 & -8\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

q-42095.name: Question 6
q-42095.worked_solution:
The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+1\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{3+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-2)-2(2-4) \\  & =-1+4 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-4)\cdot {C}_{22}+(-2)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =(-4)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-2)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4(2+3)+2(1+6) \\  & =-20+14 \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=2\cdot 3-(-6)=12.
$$

The 3rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the 3rd row, we have

|121−10−4−212001−3120|=2⋅C31+0⋅C32+0⋅C33+1⋅C34=2⋅(−1)3+1⋅|21−1−4−21120|+1⋅(−1)3+4⋅|1210−4−2−312|=2|21−1−4−21120|−|1210−4−2−312|.

Therefore,

|121−10−4−212001−3120|=2⋅3−(−6)=12.

|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|

q-130035.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the third row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(3\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|=-2\cdot 16=-32.
$$

q-70109.problem:
Compute the following determinant using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th row:

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|.
$$
q-70109.worked_solution:
Using cofactor expansion along the $4$th row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot {C}_{41}+0\cdot {C}_{42}+0\cdot {C}_{43}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{4+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{21}+0\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{2+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(9-2) \\  & =-14\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|=-4\cdot (-14)=56.
$$

The $3$rd row of the matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|+2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $3$rd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =1\cdot {C}_{31}+0\cdot {C}_{32}+5\cdot {C}_{33} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{3+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|+5\cdot (-1)^{3+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|+5|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(1-4)+5(6-3) \\  & =-3+15 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+2\cdot {C}_{22}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{23} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(5+4)+(0-2) \\  & =18-2 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 12-2\cdot 16=-20.
$$

q-70128.name: Question 10
q-70128.worked_solution:
The $2$nd row of the given matrix contains two zeros, more than any other row. So, using a Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have   

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{21}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{22}+0\cdot {C}_{23}+1\cdot {C}_{24} \\  & =(-1)\cdot (-1)^{2+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+1\cdot (-1)^{2+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}|+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the first $3\times 3$  determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & 3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+2\cdot {C}_{12}+(-1)\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2(6-2)-(-6-2) \\  & =-8-(-8) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute the second $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{11}+1\cdot {C}_{12}+2\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =1\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+(2)\cdot (-1)^{1+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(-6-2)+2(0-6) \\  & =-(-8)+2\cdot (-6) \\  & =8-12 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}|=-0+(-4)=-4.
$$

Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th column, we have

\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & -3 & 9 \\ 3 & 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| & =9\cdot {C}_{14}+0\cdot {C}_{24}+0\cdot {C}_{34}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =9\cdot (-1)^{1+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-9\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36217.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $3$rd column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 7 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 5 & 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{13}+4\cdot {C}_{23}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{43} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & -2\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

q-77500.worked_solution:
Using a cofactor expansion along the $4$th column, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{14}+5\cdot {C}_{24}+0\cdot {C}_{34}+0\cdot {C}_{44} \\  & =5\cdot (-1)^{2+4}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$
